newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S., Britain to urge Kuwait not to buy China gun.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Britain to urge Kuwait not to buy China gun.

text.p: Kuwait's key Western allies are expected to press the Gulf Arab state to reverse a decision to buy tracked Chinese self-propelled guns, diplomatic and industry sources said on Tuesday.
"You bet they (Britain and the United States) are not happy with that decision," said an industry expert. They are proposing their own weapons, saying they are superior.
William Cohen is to make his first visit to Kuwait as U.S. Defence Secretary in mid-June while British Foreign Office Minister Derek Fatchett is expected to arrive on June 23.
"I think both men are going to raise the issue and insist that Kuwait reviews its decision," said a diplomatic source, adding that Kuwait is aware of their position.

There has been no official announcement but the sources said a Kuwaiti military committee had recently picked the Chinese to equip a Kuwait Land Forces batallion with 18 howtizers with an option for a second batallion.
U.S. and British officials had priced their weapons systems at $200 million for a batallion.
"It can't be the price. The difference between the Western systems on offer and the Chinese is not that large," said a senior Western diplomat. "It is a political decision."

Since it was freed from a seven-month Iraqi occupation in 1991, Kuwait, a major arms buyer, has had a policy of awarding key weapons contracts to the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.

In competition with China, Washington, which led the Gulf War, hopes to sell Kuwait its M109 A6 Paladin. The British are pushing hard to sell the Desert AS90. South Africa has offered its wheeled LIW 155mm G6.

Kuwait has defence and cooperation pacts with China, Russia, France, Britain and the United States. All but China have won arms contracts since the Gulf war but Beijing has secured other lucrative state deals.
Some recent arms deals have been put on hold due to parliament's insistence on reviewing contracts.

The British minister is expected to discuss Kuwait's apparent freezing of a decision to buy British Aerospace Plc surface-to-surface Sea Skua missiles. Some MPs want parliament to probe the deal, made after a cheaper offer by France's Aerospatiale MM-15 was dropped.
The missiles will arm Kuwait's eight, French-made $500 million fast patrol boats ordered in 1995.
